_note: Jung, Collected Works: the passages on Ignatius and the Exercises, read in the operator's copy of the Complete Digital Edition (word search for Ignatius, Loyola, Exercitia, Spiritual Exercises, Rickaby, Izquierdo; index and bibliography pages left out; passages where 'spiritual exercises' is generic left out). Paragraph numbers read from the page, not estimated. Notes are summaries (CC BY 4.0); no text of Jung's is reproduced. Where Jung names no place in the book, the placement is editorial and the note says so. Jung quotes the Exercises in Rickaby's second edition (1923), the edition whose notes are in this apparatus.

glosses.note: The ego depends on something greater and is directed towards it as its goal; Jung hears this in the opening sentence of the Foundation, which his note gives in Latin, with a reference to Rickaby, p. 18.

'Homo creatus est' as the fundamentum of the Exercises: the self precedes the ego, which does not make itself. Jung calls this half of the psychological truth; the other half is that man also shapes what made him.

The colloquy as a technique of inner dialogue, admitted by Ignatius with one restriction: only the meditant speaks, and the answers from within are set aside as merely human. The note cites Izquierdo (1686) on the colloquy as familiar talk with Christ. Not everyone, Jung adds, is fit for such exercises.
Ruland's alchemical definition of meditatio as inner dialogue with an unseen other; Jung's note finds it very close to the colloquy of the Exercises.

Exercitia spiritualia and yoga as techniques of transformation: methods fixed in advance to bring about a definite psychic effect. Placed on Annotation 1, the book's own definition of spiritual exercises (editorial).

glosses.loc: CW 13 (Paracelsus as a Spiritual Phenomenon), §201, note
glosses.note: Paracelsus' 'imitation' of Aniadus by imagination compared with active imagination in the Exercises: consideratio, contemplatio, meditatio, ponderatio and imaginatio per sensus serve the 'realization' of what is imagined. The note sends the reader to Rickaby, pp. 40ff., the meditation on hell, and compares the contemplation of the life of Jesus.

The bitterness of the sea and of damnation: the fourth point of the fifth exercise, tasting bitter things in hell, cited from Rickaby, p. 41, beside the more lurid hell exercise of the Jesuit Sebastián Izquierdo (1686).

Imagination through the five senses (Rickaby, p. 41, the hell meditation) as the fullest possible 'realization' of the object of contemplation, which Jung sets beside the alchemist's total act of recognition.
Imitating Christ 'by use of his senses', from the first method of prayer (Rickaby, p. 215): the same argument as the previous gloss.

glosses.loc: CW 11 (Commentary on The Tibetan Book of the Great Liberation), §793
glosses.note: Ignatius used active imagination, Jung's own term for his method, in the Exercises. Jung names no paragraph; placed on the composition of place, seeing with the eye of the imagination (editorial).

The Christian contemplative of the Exercises grasps the holy image as concretely as possible, with all the senses, as the yogi solidifies what he contemplates. Placed on the application of the senses (editorial).

Exercises and yoga alike give the meditant an object and so shut out his own fantasies as worthless; the West, apart from the very limited use of the Jesuit Exercitia, has developed nothing like yoga, out of fear of the personal unconscious.
Like Shri Ramana's extinction of the ego in the self, the Exercitia subordinate self-possession to possession by Christ. Placed on the Suscipe (editorial).
Recalling his ETH course on the Exercitia, Jung speaks of the total surrender they ask for, in which one never knows whether one meets sanctity or spiritual pride. Placed on the Suscipe (editorial).
Is the Christ to whom one surrenders the Christ of the Synoptics, of the Exercitia, of a monk of Athos, of Zinzendorf? The Christ of the Exercises as one image among many.

glosses.loc: CW 8 (On the Nature of the Psyche), §395
glosses.note: From the Autobiography, not the Exercises: the bright serpent-like light full of eyes that first consoled Ignatius and was later recognized as an evil spirit, read by Jung as an image of the many luminosities of the unconscious. Placed on the rules for the enemy who comes as an angel of light (editorial).

glosses.loc: CW 7 (On the Psychology of the Unconscious), §119
glosses.note: The serpent vision, taken first for a divine and then for a diabolical visitation, as an instance of an original experience replaced by borrowed interpretation. Placed on the rules for the second week's discernment (editorial).
The serpent vision as a humanly limited interpretation of an experience, with 1 John 4:1 on testing the spirits. Placed on the second week's rules of discernment (editorial).
Nothing guarantees that the spirit is not the devil, as with Ignatius' serpens oculatus, taken first for Christ and later for the devil. Placed on the second week's rules of discernment (editorial).

As the struggle of light and darkness moved inward, Ignatius thought it necessary to make the conflict felt through drastic exercises. The note cites Rickaby, pp. 75ff., which are Rickaby's notes on the later rules of discernment for the first week, the enemy's tactics.

Jung ascribes to Ignatius the maxim that the end sanctifies the means, drawn from the authority of the Church, and sets it beside the Marxist state. The maxim is not in the Exercises; placed on the thirteenth rule for thinking with the Church (editorial).

Meditation today: a theme chosen by the meditant or set by an instructor, as in the Ignatian Exercitia; of value for concentration, not for an encounter with the unconscious. Placed on Annotation 2, on the one who gives the matter (editorial).

The Exercitia as the Western parallel to yoga: both impress fixed forms, here fixed ideas of salvation, on consciousness, which is right as long as the symbol still expresses the unconscious situation.

glosses.loc: CW 11 (Commentary on The Tibetan Book of the Dead), §854
glosses.note: Initiation methods, the Exercitia among them, anticipate natural development and put a set of traditional symbols in place of the spontaneous ones.

glosses.loc: CW 11 (Commentary on The Tibetan Book of the Great Liberation), §778
glosses.note: Compared with yoga, the Exercitia show how far behind the West is in psychological technique; but jumping into Eastern yoga is no remedy.
Protestants who take refuge in the rigorously Catholic exercises of Ignatius; the Exercises as the Western practice nearest to yoga.

glosses.loc: CW 11 (Foreword to Suzuki's Introduction to Zen Buddhism), §893
glosses.note: Two kinds of religious experience: the mystic's emptying of images, and exercises like Ignatius' that work by envisaging sacred images.
Jung recalls lecturing at the ETH for a whole year on the Spiritual Exercises (1939–40, see the ETH lectures in the works list).
